Logging of permitted privileged actions too, with path and result, so evidence exists before a reviewer asks.

questions.explanation: A hook is both a control and a source of evidence. The course's example blocks the disallowed write and logs it, and also logs every permitted privileged action, so the control and its evidence exist before a reviewer ever asks. Analogy: a building's door scanner that records only rejected badges cannot tell a manager who actually went into the server room. The rejected badges are the denials, the successful swipes are the permitted writes, and the manager's question is about the second group. Logging only denials answers a question nobody asked.

distractor_explanations.A: An instruction describes intent, and a reviewer wants a record of what happened.
distractor_explanations.B: The request is for a record of actions that were taken. Explaining denials does not show them.
distractor_explanations.C: Permitted privileged actions are the ones that changed something, so they belong in the record.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A hook blocks a file write that a fetched web page tried to trigger through hidden text. For the audit trail, which record best serves a reviewer?

options.text: The page's full HTML alone, with no record of the action or the decision taken.
The fetched source, the action that was attempted, and the fact that it was blocked.
The model's private reasoning about why it chose to write, with the page left out.
Only the final summary the user received, since blocked actions never reach the user.

questions.explanation: For prompt injection the course's defense checklist logs the fetched source, the action attempted, and the block. That record shows where the hostile instruction entered, what it tried to do, and that the control stopped it, which is the evidence a regulated review looks for.

distractor_explanations.A: Without the action and the block, the reviewer cannot see what was attempted or that it was stopped.
distractor_explanations.C: The record should identify where the instruction came from and what the control did.
distractor_explanations.D: The summary omits the attempted action and its source, which are what a reviewer needs to see.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: A team wants Claude Code to confirm, at the start of every session, that the `DEPLOY_TOKEN` environment variable is set and a required service is reachable before any work begins. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: A Stop hook, which runs each time the model finishes responding at the end of a turn in the session.
A path-scoped rules file that loads when Claude begins working on files that sit in the deployment folder.
A SessionStart hook, which runs when a session starts or resumes and can validate the environment first.
A CLAUDE.md line asking Claude to check them, since the file loads every session and is followed without exception.

questions.explanation: Hooks are bound to lifecycle events, and SessionStart runs when a session starts or resumes, which makes it the place to initialize state, validate environment variables, or confirm required services are reachable before the agent begins. Instructions in CLAUDE.md or rules files are guidance the model reads, not checks that run.

distractor_explanations.A: Stop fires at the end of a turn, long after work has begun.
distractor_explanations.B: Rules files supply guidance when matching files are used. They do not run checks at session start.
distractor_explanations.D: A CLAUDE.md line is a convention that can be followed inconsistently. A hook is what runs deterministically.

questions.source_repo: Anthropic Partner Academy / CCDV-F Official Prep (Moderate Tier)
questions.prompt: An end-to-end test of a support bot fails. Its trace shows: step 1 `retrieve` returned 0 chunks, step 2 `build_prompt` ok, step 3 `model.call` returned a generic answer, step 4 `assert` failed. The parser and call-shape tests pass. What does the trace add that the failing test alone could not?

options.text: It proves the model call is at fault, since the generic answer was produced at step 3 of the trace.
Nothing, since an end-to-end test already reports which step failed as part of its normal result output.
It shows the prompt wording is wrong, since the prompt-building step sits between retrieval and the model in the flow.
It localizes the break to step 1, the retrieval, since the end-to-end test shows only that the answer was wrong.

questions.explanation: A test says that a failure exists, and a trace shows which step produced it. An end-to-end test sees only the final output, so it is hard to localize on its own, whereas the trace records each step's output and timing and reveals that retrieval returned nothing. Analogy: a late parcel tells you the delivery failed, but the tracking log shows it never left the first depot. The failed delivery is the end-to-end failure, the tracking log is the trace, and blaming the last driver is the tempting wrong target.

distractor_explanations.A: Step 3 answered from an empty context, so it behaved as it should. The missing input came from retrieval.
distractor_explanations.B: An end-to-end test sees only the final result, which is why a trace is needed to localize the failing step.
distractor_explanations.C: The prompt step ran without error, and its input was empty. Rewording it would not repair the missing chunks.
